Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Start at the south gate because the path from the bus stop comes in beside the water tank. The gate is usually open from half past seven on weekdays. The combination lock is for the tool shed, not for this gate, so don't try that one. The gravel gets loose near the hinge, and you can catch a wheel on it. If you're bringing a cart, take the left side, where the ground is firmer.

I'm walking through with Mara, who has plot fourteen. She says, “Leave the latch resting on the hook if you're only carrying a watering can.” But if you bring a delivery through, close the gate behind you, because the rabbits from the neighboring yard have found the gap twice this spring. There's a wooden sign with the site rules just inside, and the notice board has the rota for the shared tap. Check the paper version because the online calendar sometimes shows last month's dates.

1. Check the water before you start carrying anything. The tap is halfway down the central path on the right, beside the blue rain barrel. Turn the red handle slowly and wait a moment, because the pipe takes a few seconds to fill. If it coughs air, don't force it. Just let the water run into the shallow concrete drain until it comes clear. The pressure is lower on Sunday afternoons, when a lot of people are filling cans. The tap is connected to the mains, not the rain barrel, and the barrel is there for rinsing muddy tools, not for drinking. There's a short hose on the wall, but it belongs to the shared area, so wind it back onto the bracket when you're done. If the washer drips, tell Jo in the small office rather than tightening the joint with pliers. She's got replacement washers in a labeled tin.

2. Find your plot using the painted posts, not the little wooden labels. Some labels have faded, and plot numbers fourteen and forty-one look almost the same from the path. The allotment plan is pinned by the tap, and the north arrow points toward the railway embankment. Plot fourteen is two beds past the green compost bins on the left. Mara keeps the gate to her plot open, but the narrow path through it is not a shortcut for other plots. The soil is raised at the edges, and the boards are slippery after rain. Step over at the low corner if you need to get to the bed.

There are three beds on this plot: one for beans, one for salad leaves, and one that Mara is leaving empty until she decides what to plant. She said she might put in courgettes, but she hasn't ordered the plants yet. Don't tell people they're definitely going there.

Before we work the soil, look at the weather and touch it rather than following a fixed schedule. The top inch can look dry while the ground underneath is still damp. Push a finger down beside a plant, not right against its stem. If the earth holds together lightly, it can wait. If it falls away like dust, give it a drink in the morning so the leaves have time to dry before night. Mara uses a green watering can for seedlings and a grey one for established plants. The green can has a narrow rose that softens the flow. The seedlings in the wooden tray are lettuce, not spinach. She corrected me on that last week. There are six rows, and the two nearest the fence were sown later, so they're smaller. The blue tags show the sowing dates. The handwriting is hard to read, but the newest row says April twenty-second.

3. Weed carefully before adding compost. Pull small weeds by hand after rain, when the roots come out more easily. For deep-rooted weeds, use the fork kept under the bench and loosen the soil around the root. Don't chop it into pieces, because some weeds grow back from fragments. Mara keeps a bucket for weeds with no seed heads and a separate bag for anything already flowering. The bucket goes on the compost heap, but the bag is taken to the green waste collection point by the road. Don't put diseased leaves on the heap either; the site's heap does not get hot enough to deal with every plant problem.

Use a thin layer of finished compost around the beans and keep it a couple of centimeters away from the stems. There's a yellow scoop hanging inside the tool shed, and one scoop per bed is enough for this visit. The compost is dark and crumbly, but it can contain small twigs, so spread it by hand rather than tipping a whole heap into one place.

4. Tie up the climbing beans only when the stems are long enough to reach the support. The canes are arranged as two rows with a crossbar, and soft green twine lies in the biscuit tin on the bench. Make a loose loop below a leaf joint and leave room for the stem to thicken. Mara says, “A tight knot is harder on the plant than a windy day.” If you find a broken cane, don't push it back into the soil where the roots are. Mark the spot with a spare cane and ask before replacing it. The neighboring plot has spare bamboo, but it is not shared stock, and the owner is only here on Wednesdays. The bean flowers attract bees, so don't spray anything on them, even if a leaf has a few holes.

5. Finish by putting tools away and writing down anything the next person needs to know. Scrape soil off the fork with the wooden scraper and rinse the watering can at the drain. Don't leave it full, because the water can turn stale in warm weather. Return the hose to its bracket, shut the shed door, and check that the gate latch is back on its hook. The notice board has a small notebook for repairs. Write the date and the item rather than leaving a message on the back of the rules sheet. If the tap is leaking, note whether it drips with the handle closed and tell Jo at the office when she's there on Tuesday or Thursday.

There is a first aid box inside the shed on the top shelf, and the site phone number is taped inside its lid. The phone is not for routine gardening questions. The office is closed on public holidays, so leave a note in the box by the gate if you need a reply. Next day, before you leave, look back at the plot from the path and check that the young plants are not buried under compost and that the empty bed stays empty today. The forecast says light rain overnight, but it may pass north of us, so I would check the soil again tomorrow morning rather than assuming the rain reached this end of town.

My neighbor Nadia had told me the cooperative was short of volunteers after their regular attendant hurt her wrist. I got there on Thursday just after one thirty with a canvas bag of towels and a smaller bag of shirts. The place was in a converted shop beside the pharmacy, and the bell above the door kept ringing whenever somebody came in. There were six washers along the back wall, four dryers by the windows, and a folding table made from two doors set on trestles. The room smelled like warm cotton and orange cleaner. Nadia waved from behind the counter and said, “If you can read a label and keep an eye on the clock, you're already useful.” I laughed because I was not sure she was serious, but she handed me an apron anyway.

1. Arrival and intake. First, we had to sort the drop-offs by customer name and by the time each person expected to collect them. Second, we checked pockets and read care labels, and if a label was missing, we put the item in a separate basket instead of guessing. Third, Nadia showed me the paper cards they clipped to each mesh bag. The cards had a name, a phone number, the number of pieces, and a note if anything needed to stay out of the dryer. I wrote down “Mrs. Chen, two sheets, one pillowcase, cold wash,” and then had to ask Nadia whether pillowcases counted as one piece each. She said yes, even when they arrived rolled up inside a sheet. A man called Mr. Ellis brought in a work jacket with a small tear at the cuff. He asked if we could wash it gently and leave the tear alone. We wrote that down, and he nodded before he left. Nobody at the counter promised to mend it.

We had a rush around two because three people arrived within a few minutes, and I put one card in the wrong slot. I noticed it when the name on the card did not match the number written on the bag, so I stopped before putting anything into a machine. Nadia said, “Good catch,” and we checked the receipts together. The bag belonged to Lena Ortiz, not Lila Ortiz, and the phone numbers ended in 18 and 81. After that, I read every name out loud while Nadia checked it against the receipt. One customer asked whether she could bring her own unscented detergent next time. Nadia said she could, as long as it was in a sealed container and clearly marked. We had a shelf with three shared detergents, a small bottle of stain remover, and a jar of clothespins. I was surprised how much of the job was keeping track of little details rather than operating machines.

2. The machine problem. The first washer finished just before three, but its door stayed locked even after the cycle light went dark. I waited a minute, then tried the handle once and stopped because I did not want to force it. The machine had a yellow service sticker with a number, and Nadia called the repair line while I checked the other loads. She told the person on the phone that the washer was a front loader, gave the model number written on the sticker, and said the display showed no error code. I could hear the person asking questions, but I did not hear what they recommended. Nadia wrote something on the back of an old receipt and said we would leave that machine alone until she could check the instructions. She moved the waiting bag to a chair and told the customer there might be a delay. He said, “That's okay, I can come back after dinner.” We put a note beside his card so nobody would forget to call him if the timing changed.

While we waited, I learned how they handled shared supplies. Each volunteer wrote down detergent, gloves, and cleaning cloths taken from the cupboard, not because anyone suspected people of taking too much, but because the monthly budget was tight. The ledger had dates going back to January, with pencil marks where someone had corrected a count. Nadia said the cooperative charged by load size, not by weight, and displayed the prices on a board by the entrance. The money covered rent, water, electricity, and replacement parts, and they kept a separate envelope for customers who asked for help paying. I asked how they decided who could use that envelope. Nadia said they spoke privately with the person and worked it out case by case; she did not give me a formula. I appreciated that she did not turn it into a speech. Meanwhile, I wiped down the folding table and found a single red mitten under one of the benches. We put it in the lost-and-found tin with the date written on a strip of masking tape.

3. Closing up. By five, the room was quieter, though two dryers were still running. We folded the towels together on the table and set aside a pale blue shirt because its tag said to hang it up. I almost folded it with the rest, then caught the tag before I made the crease. Nadia showed me where the wooden hangers were, and I put the shirt in a paper cover with its customer card. The man with the work jacket came back while we were checking the pickup shelf. His jacket was still being washed, so Nadia told him it was not ready and repeated the note about the cuff. He said he understood and left without seeming upset. Before I went, I wrote my name and the hours I had helped in the volunteer book. Nadia asked if I could come again the following month, and I said maybe, depending on my schedule. I carried my two bags home, one lighter because I had left the towels for the cooperative to finish.
